authors: Klaus M. Miller, Karlo Lukic, Bernd Skiera
title: The Impact of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) on Online Tracking
venue: arXiv:2411.06862 (econ.GN); earlier NBER conference/working paper versions
method: difference-in-differences on balanced panel of 294 publishers (WhoTracks.me data, May 2017-Dec 2019), EU publishers vs unaffected control
outcomes: number and type of third-party trackers per website
headline: GDPR reduced about four trackers per publisher, a 14.79% decrease relative to the control group, mainly privacy-invasive trackers; little effect on advertising trackers.
summary_plain: Websites covered by the GDPR added fewer tracking tools than comparable websites outside its reach, especially the trackers that collect and share personal data.
quality: Credible DiD with control group; modest sample of 294 publishers; tracker counts from one data provider

authors: Klaus M. Miller, Bernd Skiera, Julia Schmitt
title: The Impact of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) on Online Usage Behavior
method: generalized synthetic control on visits to 6,387 websites in 24 industries and 13 countries, 11 months before and 19 months after enforcement
outcomes: website visits, unique visitors, visits per visitor
headline: Weekly visits fell by 4.88% within 3 months and 10.02% after 18 months, driven by fewer unique visitors (-6.61%); about a quarter of websites gained.
summary_plain: After the GDPR, websites affected by it got about 10% fewer visits after a year and a half, mostly because fewer people visited, although some sites gained users at others' expense.
period_geography: 2017-2019; 13 countries, EU users/EU websites vs others
quality: Strong causal design on very large data; traffic data from a single analytics provider

authors: Raffaele Congiu, Lorien Sabatino, Geza Sapi
title: The Impact of Privacy Regulation on Web Traffic: Evidence From the GDPR
method: difference-in-differences on traffic data for ~5,000 web domains in Europe and the US
headline: GDPR reduced website traffic by about 15% in the long run, with smallest and largest sites losing most and effects amplified after the first major fine.
summary_plain: European websites lost roughly 15% of their visitors after the GDPR compared with US sites, and the drop grew after regulators began fining firms.
quality: DiD with US control; traffic estimates from third-party panel (SimilarWeb-type) data

authors: Miguel Godinho de Matos, Idris Adjerid
title: Consumer Consent and Firm Targeting After GDPR: The Case of a Large Telecom Provider
method: field experiment around GDPR-compliant consent elicitation at a large European telecom provider
outcomes: consumer opt-in rates, sales, marketing efficacy, contractual lock-in
headline: Opt-in for data uses rose once GDPR-compliant consent was elicited, and sales, marketing efficacy and contractual lock-in increased, while consumers kept restricting sensitive uses.
summary_plain: When a telecom firm asked customers for consent the GDPR way, more customers agreed to share data, and the firm then sold more through better-targeted marketing.
quality: Experimental variation within a single firm; external validity limited

authors: Knut Blind, Crispin Niebel, Christian Rammer
title: The impact of the EU General data protection regulation on product innovation
method: conditional difference-in-differences with firm fixed effects on German innovation survey (Mannheim Innovation Panel)
headline: GDPR led to a substantial shift from radical to incremental product innovation in German firms.
summary_plain: German firms affected by the GDPR did more improving of existing products and less developing of entirely new ones, as compliance absorbed resources.
quality: DiD on representative firm survey panel; treatment intensity self-reported

authors: Vincent Lefrere, Logan Warberg, Cristobal Cheyre, Veronica Marotta, Alessandro Acquisti
title: Does Privacy Regulation Harm Content Providers? A Longitudinal Analysis of the Impact of the GDPR
method: difference-in-differences on longitudinal panel of EU and US news and media websites
outcomes: tracking, consent mechanisms, content production, quality proxies, traffic, survival, monetization
headline: EU news sites cut tracking more than US sites and saw fewer page views per user, but no negative effect on new content provision, content quality, survival or monetization.
summary_plain: European news websites collected less data after the GDPR but kept producing as much content of similar quality as US sites, and did not close more often.
quality: DiD with US control and many outcomes; sample limited to news/media sites

title: Short-term Impacts of the GDPR on Firm Performance
method: difference-in-differences on firm-level financial panel of European and US companies 2014-2018
headline: Profit margins of EU data-intensive firms rose about 1.7-3.4 percentage points less than US counterparts in the first GDPR year; SMEs hit hardest, no difference for very large firms.
summary_plain: In the GDPR's first year, European companies that rely heavily on data saw their profit margins grow less than similar US companies, with smaller firms affected most.
quality: DiD with US control; only one post-period year; data-intensity classification by industry

authors: James Bessen, Stephen Michael Impink, Lydia Reichensperger, Robert Seamans
title: GDPR and the Importance of Data to AI Startups
venue: SSRN working paper / BU Technology & Policy Research Initiative
method: survey of AI startups in more than 25 countries with regression analysis
outcomes: data deletion, resource reallocation, new GDPR positions
headline: Nearly three quarters of surveyed AI startups reported deleting some data because of GDPR; firms with European customers were more likely to create GDPR positions or reallocate resources.
summary_plain: Most AI start-ups surveyed said they had deleted data to comply with the GDPR, and those selling in Europe more often had to shift staff and money to compliance.
quality: Self-reported survey, no counterfactual; moderate sample

authors: Martin Degeling, Christine Utz, Christopher Lentzsch, Henry Hosseini, Florian Schaub, Thorsten Holz
title: We Value Your Privacy ... Now Take Some Cookies: Measuring the GDPR's Impact on Web Privacy
method: longitudinal web measurement of the 500 most popular websites in each of 28 EU states (6,579 sites)
headline: By May 2018, 84.5% of websites had privacy policies (72.6% of existing ones updated) and 62.1% displayed cookie consent notices, 16% more than in January 2018.
summary_plain: Around the GDPR start date, most popular European websites updated their privacy policies and many more began showing cookie banners.
quality: Large before/after crawl; no control group; measures form rather than substance of compliance

authors: Midas Nouwens, Ilaria Liccardi, Michael Veale, David Karger, Lalana Kagal
title: Dark Patterns after the GDPR: Scraping Consent Pop-ups and Demonstrating their Influence
method: web scrape of consent pop-ups of five main CMPs on UK top-10,000 sites (n=680) plus field experiment with 40 participants
outcomes: compliance of consent designs, consent rates
headline: Only 11.8% of consent pop-ups met minimal requirements based on EU law; removing the first-page opt-out raised consent by 22-23 percentage points.
summary_plain: Almost nine in ten cookie consent pop-ups on major UK websites did not meet basic legal requirements, and design tricks clearly pushed people into agreeing.
quality: Compliance measurement with clear criteria; small experiment; UK only

authors: Bernhard Ganglmair, Julia Krämer, Jacopo Gambato
title: Regulatory Compliance With Limited Enforceability: Evidence From Privacy Policies
venue: ZEW Discussion Paper No. 24-012 / CRC TR 224 DP 547
method: text-as-data analysis of a large panel of German firms' privacy policies before and after GDPR, with inspection model
outcomes: disclosure volume and readability of privacy policies
headline: Firms increased disclosure volume in privacy policies after GDPR but readability did not improve; better-funded data protection authorities induced better readability.
summary_plain: German companies wrote longer privacy policies after the GDPR, but they did not get any easier to read, except where regulators had more money to enforce.
quality: Large text panel; before/after with heterogeneity, no clean control group

title: Special Eurobarometer 487a: The General Data Protection Regulation
outcomes: awareness of GDPR, data rights and data protection authorities
headline: 73% had heard of at least one of six GDPR rights, 67% knew about the GDPR and 57% about their national data protection authority; 62% worried about lacking control of data online.
summary_plain: A year after the GDPR, two-thirds of Europeans had heard of it and most knew at least one of their new rights, but many still felt they lacked control over their data.
quality: Large representative survey; awareness only, no pre-GDPR baseline in same form
interested_party: European Commission (commissioned by the act's author)

title: Mandate to overblock? Understanding the impact of the European Union's Article 17 on copyright content moderation on YouTube
method: comparison of YouTube takedowns and genre diversity (Stirling dual-concept diversity index) in Germany vs France, exploiting Germany's 5-month-earlier Article 17 implementation
outcomes: copyright-related video takedowns, cultural supply diversity on YouTube
headline: Over 2019-2022, takedowns in copyright-prone categories differed significantly between Germany and France, and content diversity (genres, videos, subscribers) fell in both, more so in Germany.
summary_plain: Comparing Germany, which applied the new upload rules earlier, with France, the authors found more removal of copyright-sensitive videos and a larger drop in the variety of content on YouTube in Germany.
quality: Quasi-experimental comparison of two countries using reused data; descriptive inference, no formal DiD; open access

authors: Leon van Eendenburg, Jolanta Suárez (data.europa.eu / Publications Office)
title: High-value datasets: Cross-country findability and comparability of metadata
venue: data.europa.eu study, Publications Office of the EU, doi:10.2830/0033148
method: pilot audit of 24 high-value datasets in Denmark, Estonia, Latvia and Finland against Implementing Regulation 2023/138 metadata requirements (April-May 2024)
outcomes: availability, findability and metadata quality of high-value datasets
headline: Of 24 high-value datasets assessed, 20 were found, 3 were gated and 1 unavailable; 14 were easily findable on data.europa.eu and 8 did not reference the regulation.
summary_plain: A spot check of 24 key public datasets in four countries found most were available but many were hard to find or poorly labelled, just before the EU rules took effect.
quality: Small pilot sample, conducted just before application date; descriptive only
interested_party: European Commission (data.europa.eu, author of the act)

authors: Sean Ennis, Marc Ivaldi, Vicente Lagos
title: Price parity clauses for hotel room booking: Empirical evidence from regulatory change
method: difference-in-differences on hotel chain transaction data, exploiting EU narrowing of OTA parity clauses and French/German full bans, with non-EU comparison
outcomes: direct vs OTA room prices by hotel segment
headline: Restricting parity clauses made direct-channel hotel sales significantly cheaper than OTA sales for mid-level and luxury hotels (opposite for budget hotels), mainly from the move to narrow parity.
summary_plain: After competition authorities limited booking platforms' 'best price' clauses, rooms booked directly with mid-range and luxury hotels became cheaper relative to platform prices.
quality: Natural experiments with external control; concerns predecessor enforcement that VBER 2022 codified (wide parity excluded from block exemption)

title: Vertical contracting and price parity agreements: evidence from hotels in Europe
method: difference-in-differences exploiting 2014 German ban and 2015 Sweden/Italy/France actions on OTA price parity clauses
headline: Regulatory actions against price parity clauses were associated with hotel price decreases of 9-15%, largest for lower-quality hotels.
summary_plain: Hotel prices fell by roughly a tenth in countries where authorities stopped booking platforms from imposing 'best price' clauses.
quality: DiD on predecessor national interventions (not VBER 2022 itself); unpublished student working paper

authors: European Competition Network (Commission and 10 national competition authorities)
title: Report on the monitoring exercise carried out in the online hotel booking sector by EU competition authorities in 2016
venue: European Commission / ECN, April 2017 (press release by Autorité de la concurrence)
method: before/after comparison of OTA price differentiation plus survey of hotels in 10 Member States
outcomes: price differentiation across OTAs, hotel awareness of parity changes
headline: Moving from wide to narrow parity clauses led to increased price differentiation between OTAs in most countries; almost half of surveyed hotels were unaware of the changes (30% in France and Germany).
summary_plain: Competition authorities found that after booking platforms dropped their broadest 'best price' clauses, hotels started charging different prices on different platforms, though many hotels did not know they could.
quality: Descriptive monitoring of predecessor enforcement; authorities evaluating own remedies
interested_party: Competition authorities evaluating their own remedies

title: Digitalization and Cross-Border Tax Fraud: Evidence from E-Invoicing in Italy
method: difference-in-differences on product-level intra-EU trade gaps (mirror trade data) around Italy's 2019 mandatory e-invoicing
outcomes: cross-border VAT fraud proxied by trade gaps; revenue loss
headline: Mandatory e-invoicing in Italy significantly reduced cross-border VAT fraud, cutting Italian revenue loss by an estimated EUR 0.6-1 billion in 2019.
summary_plain: When Italy made electronic invoices compulsory, signs of cross-border VAT fraud fell noticeably, saving the state up to about a billion euros in the first year.
period_geography: around 2019; Italy vs other EU countries
quality: Credible quasi-experimental design on a national predecessor of ViDA's e-invoicing/digital reporting requirements, not ViDA itself

title: Transparency Report as per Article 8 of the Terrorist Content Online Regulation and Monitoring Report as per Article 21(1) - Year under review 2025
method: administrative statistics on removal orders, removal requests, objections and Article 5 procedures
outcomes: removal orders issued and complied with, removal requests, compliance rates
headline: In 2025 the Bundeskriminalamt issued 245 removal orders (99.2% implemented, 237 fewer than in 2024) and 29,792 voluntary removal requests (93.2% implemented vs 87.4% in 2024).
summary_plain: Germany's police used the regulation's binding one-hour removal orders a few hundred times in 2025 and platforms almost always complied, while far more content was taken down through voluntary requests.
quality: Official counts from the competent authority; outputs only, no measure of effect on terrorist content availability
interested_party: National competent authority reporting on its own activity
